fields.Core Themes JSON: [{"title": "Astro-Yoga and the Body's Sky Clock", "body": "Emily Ridout describes herself as an astro-yoga specialist who helps people pair their astrology chart with the energy body and the physical body. She says yoga, astrology and medicine have been linked for thousands of years, and that she teaches public classes timed to the stars as well as personal work with a birth chart. Chance says rooting astrology in movement helps people remember what a screen cannot, while Emily says easing toward a north node through the body can make a big life leap feel aligned instead of shocking."}, {"title": "Armoring, Rigidity and Suppleness", "body": "Chance brings in Wilhelm Reich's idea of character armoring, describing a personality that stiffens alongside the muscles, with that rigidity amounting to stuck energy and a filter between the body and the world. He argues that becoming supple and soft is the truest kind of strength, because what is flexible is harder to break than what is rigid, and that loosening up frees mental energy. Emily replies that her practices tend to bring each person what they need, loosening the rigid and strengthening the over-flexible."}, {"title": "Eclipse Season and Questioning Your Truth", "body": "Emily explains that lunar eclipses fall at full moons and solar eclipses at new moons, with eclipse season arriving about every six months when the sun nears the lunar nodes, which at recording sit in Gemini and Sagittarius. She says the energetic wave lasts roughly six months, though she asks listeners to take that with a grain of salt. Her main message is that we mistake our relative truth for the ultimate one, so she asks everyone to problematize their own truth, and Chance links this to Reich doubting his own certainty."}, {"title": "Enemies, Energy and Compassion", "body": "Emily says that agreeing to let someone be your enemy hands them a big portion of your energy, and she keeps reminding herself that the person or media corporation we fight is usually not the true enemy. Chance adds that dwelling on an enemy is a way of loving it, that letting go may reveal our own saboteur, and that real hurdles still sometimes demand boundaries. Emily balances this with Gemini's positive side, the blindfolded elephant parable, which she says opens us to compassion, and a workshop tale of a demon who hated Krishna until he saw only the divine."}, {"title": "Dragons, Treasure and the Leap North", "body": "Chance retells, as best he can from a Telegram friend, the myth of Rahu and Ketu, a demon who sipped the elixir of immortality before a god severed its head, while Emily says she sticks to the Shaivite tradition and sees the nodes as places we can get stuck or fear to go. Her retelling of Autobiography of a Yogi, where two young men travel without money and are provided for, leads her to ask what treasure your dragon should sit on. Chance pairs it with stepping off a cliff toward the north node."}]
fields.Intro Paragraph 1: Emily Ridout returns to help us retrospect on the powerful eclipse energy we felt at the end of May and the murky mental situation of Mercury going retrograde with the sun in Gemini. You'll also find out more about Emily's Astro-yoga classes and this knowledge might help you bend instead of break during turbulent times.

fields.Plus Core Themes JSON: [{"title": "Mercury Retrograde Through Gemini", "body": "Emily Ridout explains why Mercury retrograde irritates so many people: a society that prizes speed expects prompt replies and smooth technology, while the retrograde asks intellect, communication and devices to turn inward for reflection. She calls it doubly hard because Mercury is backing through quick, Mercurial Gemini. Chance, who had just juggled a glitchy call setup, shares his own method: stop treating it as something happening to him, simplify, stay present, and let things come through without frustration, a patience he says an airy sun sign has had to learn."}, {"title": "A Three-Card Draw for the Moment", "body": "Chance opens the second hour with a daily draw: I Ching 19, Approach, which he reads as earth over heaven and the arrival of something new, then the Magician, then Bat from a set of Native American medicine cards, which he links to shamanic rebirth and echolocation. Emily, who reads traditional tarot, notes that 19 is the Sun there, which she describes as a reborn self awakening to solar consciousness, and she says Manly P. Hall's books imply 42 whenever 40 is written, calling it a secret encoding of life."}, {"title": "The Magician, Will and Water", "body": "Emily reads the Magician as the quality of will, or tapas: the single-pointed ability to direct the subconscious consciously, with one arm raised to draw superconsciousness into material reality. In the schools she studies, she says, the subconscious is water, the way to divine source, reached through gentleness rather than force, and she uses the Lovers card as a three-part picture of the psyche. Chance adds that will and wheel are etymologically similar, so manifesting will means aligning with the wheel of nature, and he says modern psychology's idea of the unconscious becomes a cop-out when it serves as an excuse."}, {"title": "Chakras, Emptiness and the Time Chakra", "body": "Chance offers a personal theory, with the caveat that he could be wrong, that the I Ching's hexagram lines map onto the chakras and leave open space at the solar plexus. He recalls a Taoist idea that a vessel is useful by its emptiness and says an empty backpack feels light. Emily adds that the sun is exalted in the third chakra, that speech is how creation is made, and that roots must be tended first. Chance also calls the crown the time chakra, linking constriction there to habits that eat time."}, {"title": "Choose One Aim and Create What You Want", "body": "Emily argues that the Magician teaches choice: you can do any one thing but not everything at once, so direct yourself, and she says that by doing one thing the others you wanted often get done too. She urges people who feel worn down by what they oppose to look at what they do want and build it. Chance agrees that we need not fight what is evil so much as participate in something better, and urges going all in, treating the effort as a guarantee rather than a gamble, and notes that the Magician is also called the juggler in some decks."}]
